summary: Describes the problem of securing Neighbor Discovery Proxy, which lets a device answer on behalf of another that isn't on the link, as in Mobile IPv6. Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) assumes the advertiser owns the address, which a proxy does not, so the two do not work together today. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A secretary answers the phone for their boss. A security check that insists only the boss may speak makes that hard, and this explains why.

questions: why send does not work with nd proxy
send and neighbor discovery proxy conflict
subtitle: Why secure neighbor discovery and address proxying are hard to combine

tldr.problem: IPv6 networks use Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) to prevent spoofing, but it requires an advertiser to own the address it advertises. Neighbor Discovery Proxies advertise on behalf of absent devices, breaking SEND's assumption.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC analyzes scenarios where proxying and SEND conflict (Mobile IPv6, bridge-like proxies) and describes potential approaches to make them work together, including router authorization, certificate delegation, and cryptographic solutions.
tldr.outcome: It identifies the challenges without proposing a standard fix, leaving the resolution to future work in protocol design and security architecture.

facts.label: Problem introduced
facts.value: Interaction between SEND (RFC 3971) and Neighbor Discovery Proxies (RFC 4389)

today: RFC 5909 is an Informational problem statement published in July 2010. It has not been obsoleted or updated, meaning the problem remains unsolved. Various standards have evolved to work around this issue (such as Proxy Mobile IPv6, RFC 5213), but a general, standardized solution combining full SEND security with arbitrary proxy Neighbor Discovery has not been standardized.

sections.title: Address Proxying and Security in IPv6
sections.content:
Neighbor Discovery is how IPv6 devices on a local network find each other and determine which device owns which address. Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND), defined in RFC 3971, adds cryptographic protection using Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGAs). In SEND, an address's owner proves ownership by signing Neighbor Discovery messages with a private key corresponding to that address.

Neighbor Discovery Proxies allow one device to advertise reachability for another device that is not present on the link. A proxy answers neighbor solicitations on behalf of an absent device, directing traffic through itself to reach the remote device. This is essential for Mobile IPv6 (where a Home Agent proxies for a Mobile Node away from home) and for extending IPv6 prefixes across multiple links.

The problem: SEND requires the address advertiser to possess the private key that generated the address. A proxy, by definition, does not own the proxied address and cannot satisfy this requirement.
sections.eli5: Neighbor Discovery is how devices on a network say 'I'm here, what's your address?' SEND adds a security check: only you can say you own your address. A proxy is a helper that says 'I'll speak for that absent device.' A proxy can't prove it owns another device's address with that device's private key.

sections.title: Why Proxying Is Needed
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 allows a mobile node to move between networks while keeping the same IPv6 address. When the node is away from home, its Home Agent stays on the home network and acts as a proxy, answering Neighbor Discovery messages on the mobile node's behalf. Without this proxy function, other devices on the home network cannot send packets to the mobile node's home address.

Another use case is link extension: when a single IPv6 prefix spans multiple network segments, proxies relay Neighbor Discovery messages between segments, acting like bridges at the IP layer rather than the link layer. A third scenario is security gateways in IKEv2 networks, which assign addresses dynamically to remote clients and must proxy Neighbor Discovery to route packets to those clients.

All three scenarios require proxies to advertise addresses they do not own. Without SEND protection, these proxied addresses become vulnerable to spoofing, but adding SEND protection seems impossible under the current rules.
sections.eli5: A traveling employee wants to keep their work address even when they leave the office. The office reception desk answers calls for them. A network link gets split across rooms, and a device in one room helps route messages to the other. A remote worker's office gateway assigns them a temporary network address. All need a helper to say 'the employee is reachable through me,' but SEND says 'you can only speak for yourself.'

sections.title: The Problem Across Different Scenarios
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6: A Home Agent (the proxy) holds a security association with the Mobile Node but does not have the private key used to generate the Mobile Node's Cryptographically Generated Address (CGA). When the Mobile Node moves away, the Home Agent cannot send SEND-signed Neighbor Advertisements for the Mobile Node's home address. Worse, if other hosts have created secure Neighbor Cache Entries for the Mobile Node's address, only an unsecure advertisement can update them, which violates SEND security rules. A rogue proxy could then spoof the address until the authentic entry times out.

Bridge-like proxies rewrite link-layer addresses and flags in Neighbor Discovery messages while forwarding them between segments. Any modification breaks a SEND digital signature. Moreover, bridge-like proxies retain the original source address of the message; they cannot sign it with their own CGA (which SEND requires for the source address to match the signer's address and the target address of Neighbor Advertisements). Authorization mechanisms based on SEND routers require explicit delegation, which conflicts with the zero-configuration goal of simple proxying.

Duplicate Address Detection (DAD) also becomes problematic: a proxy must perform DAD checks for a proxied address before advertising it, but cannot generate a SEND-signed Neighbor Solicitation for an address it does not own.
sections.eli5: When a Mobile Node is away, the Home Agent can't prove 'this address is theirs' with their private key. Bridge-like proxies must change message details, which breaks the signature. Checking if an address is unique (DAD) requires proving ownership the proxy doesn't have.

sections.title: Potential Paths Forward
sections.content:
The RFC outlines multiple approaches without settling on a single solution. Router-based authorization allows SEND routers (which are already trusted to distribute routing information) to implicitly authorize proxies to advertise addresses within their network. This requires no explicit signaling between the Mobile Node and the Home Agent.

Per-address authorization requires the Mobile Node to sign a certificate delegating authority to the proxy (the Home Agent) for a specific address and time period. The Mobile Node sends this certificate during Binding Update, allowing the Home Agent to generate signed Neighbor Advertisements. This requires developing a new message exchange mechanism.

Cryptographic approaches such as ring signatures could allow multiple parties to sign a message with any member's private key while requiring all members' public keys to verify. This would let a proxy sign on behalf of a group without possessing the specific address owner's key, but such algorithms are not yet widely trusted in the security community.

Bridge-like proxies face distinct challenges. Authorization delegation between proxies and hosts, multiple levels of proxy nesting, routing infrastructure delegation, and local trust domains all present different requirements. The RFC also discusses whether to secure proxies for unsecured addresses (addresses without CGA protection).
sections.eli5: Several ideas exist: trust router announcements to include proxy authority, have the true owner sign a permission slip for the proxy, use fancy cryptography that lets multiple people sign the same message, or build local trust zones. Each has tradeoffs.

sections.title: Security Challenges
sections.content:
Implementing secured proxy Neighbor Discovery introduces new attack surfaces. Router trust could be exploited if a router is compromised (the 'Good Router Goes Bad' attack); a malicious router could authorize rogue proxies.

Certificate transport creates a bootstrapping problem: for Mobile IPv6, the Mobile Node needs to send a certificate to the Home Agent before the tunnel is established, but the tunnel is created during the binding process. If certificates must travel through this tunnel, a chicken-and-egg situation arises.

Timekeeping attacks exploit SEND's timestamp validation. An attacker could gather Neighbor Advertisement messages while the Mobile Node is at home, then replay them later with valid timestamps. Unless certificate-based authorization includes timestamp validation that is fresh, such replayed messages could override newer advertisements. The RFC describes how an attacker might save DAD messages every second while a node is present, creating a sequence of valid-looking advertisements to replay later.
sections.eli5: A bad router could claim fake proxies are authorized. Sending certificates to a proxy before the connection is ready is tricky. An attacker could record old messages and play them back later, fooling devices into thinking the proxy is still the right answer.
